Ethelred Wade.narrative: I have fished these reed channels since I was a boy, and I know every cut and pool of them better than the palm of my hand. My father kept the village nets before me, and I keep them now: mended, tarred and counted, so that no man of Reedmoor goes out with a hole in his mesh. The works at Kettlebridge send their smoke down the valley on an east wind and it lies on the reeds like a grey blanket; I have said so at the cook-fire more than once. Leofrun and I have raised one son, Godric, who is a better fisherman than I was at his age, and I would see him settled with a boat and a wife before I am too stiff to help him get it.

memories.gist: My father put the village nets in my hands the summer I turned twenty, and told me a net is a promise to every boat in Reedmoor.
The Lean Year came and the barley plots failed with the blight, and we ate reed-root bread and traded our last smoked fish for a basket of Brackenford grain.
Godric came home with his first good catch off the reeds and I pretended not to be proud, and Leofrun laughed at me for it.
The Kettlebridge smoke lay on the reeds for three days last summer and the fish tasted of it; I said at the cook-fire the works should answer for it.
The Coombes took the Lakemead and pay Nell in grain, and I said at the common table that at least the meadow is being worked.

stances.why: A net is a promise to every boat in Reedmoor, and I am the one who keeps it.
It lies on the reeds and sours the fish, and they never asked us leave for it.
A fisherman with no boat is a hired hand all his life; I want better for my son.
Brannock's cart and the Fernhollow pedlar are how our fish becomes grain; cheat them and we starve.
After the Lean Year I count what is in the store before I sleep, every night.

Ethelred Wade.calling: I keep Reedmoor's nets whole, so no man goes out with a hole in his mesh.

Leofrun Wade.narrative: I keep the barley plots above the reeds and the vegetable rows behind the house, and I know to the basket what they will give and what they will not. Since the Lean Year I have not trusted a full store to stay full, and I count it at night when Ethelred is asleep. I have sold barley to Brackenford's store against the debt, as we all have, and there is less left than I would like with the cough going through the village. Hilda and I nurse the sick between us, and I sit with them and think about the grain.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I measured out the last of the barley in cupfuls and told no one how little was left.
I carried a basket of our barley to Brackenford's store against the debt and came home with a receipt and an empty sack.
Godric was small and I taught him the planting songs in the plot above the reeds, and he still hums them when he rows out.
I sat up three nights with a reed-cutter's child through a fever with Hilda, and the child lived.
The cough came into the reeds this autumn and I heard it in the next house before I heard it in mine.

stances.why: The Lean Year taught me that a full store is a story people tell themselves.
Hilda and I are the ones who can, and a village that lets its sick lie is no village.
It is owed, and a debt unpaid comes back at the gate with guards behind it.
She is steady and hard-working, and a match would settle him.
Elmwick and the Coombes can argue; I need the meadow's cheese and not its quarrel.

Leofrun Wade.secret: She has quietly held back a small jar of barley in the roof thatch, against a winter she fears more than she says.

Leofrun Wade.calling: I keep the barley plots honest and counted, and I sit with the sick while I think on the grain.

Godric Wade.narrative: I fish the deep water off the reeds from my father's boat, and every time I row out I am thinking of the day I will row out in my own. I have courted Wyn Sedge since the spring and we suit each other, but her mother has not given her word, and I know why: a man with no boat is a poor bargain. I owe Brannock Sedge for a share of a net and I mean to pay it before I ask Nell for anything. The cough is in the village and my mother counts the grain at night; I fish harder for it.

memories.gist: My father put the oars in my hands on the reed channel the summer I turned twelve and let me row the whole way home.
The Lean Year: I was a boy and I remember the reed-root bread and my mother measuring barley in cupfuls.
I brought home my first good catch off the deep water and my father pretended not to be proud, and my mother laughed at him.
Wyn and I walked the shingle at low tide in the spring and she said she did not mind waiting for a boat, and I minded for her.
Brannock Sedge sold me a share of a net on a handshake and I have not paid him yet; it sits on me like a stone.

stances.why: A fisherman who crews for others is never his own man, and Wyn's mother knows it.
Brannock gave me the net on a handshake and I will not have it said I did not pay.
The cough is in the village and my mother counts the grain; the catch is what stands between us and a thin spring.
I will not take Wyn without her mother's blessing, however long it takes.
The deep water off the reeds is where the money is, and my father's channels only take me so far.

pastimes: rowing out to the deep water off the reeds whenever the weather lets him

Godric Wade.calling: I fish the deep water, and one day I mean to row out in a boat that is mine.
